## Introduction

This report compares [`final_script_AA.R`](../scripts/final_script_AA.R) and
[`codex_script.R`](../scripts/codex_script.R), which create the country-year
files `final_list.csv` and `final_data_codex.csv`. It asks whether the two
workflows produce equivalent analytical data and which is more reproducible.
The comparison uses `iso` and `year` as the country-year identifier. Neither
source script nor either output file was changed for this report.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

processed_dir <- if (dir.exists("data/processed")) "data/processed" else "../data/processed"
aa <- read.csv(file.path(processed_dir, "final_list.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
codex <- read.csv(file.path(processed_dir, "final_data_codex.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
key <- c("iso", "year")
shared <- merge(aa, codex, by = key, suffixes = c("_aa", "_codex"))

match_fields <- data.frame(
  AA_output = c("gdp_1000", "oecd", "pop_dens", "urban", "age_dep", "male_edu",
                "temp", "rainfall_1000", "matmor", "infmor", "neomor", "un5mor",
                "armed_conflict_lag1"),
  Codex_output = c("gdp_1000", "oecd", "pop_dens", "urban", "age_dep", "male_edu",
                   "temp", "rainfall_1000", "maternal_mortality", "infant_mortality",
                   "neonatal_mortality", "under5_mortality", "armed_conflict")
)
mismatch_count <- function(x, y) {
  same <- (is.na(x) & is.na(y)) | (!is.na(x) & !is.na(y) & x == y)
  sum(!same)
}
match_fields$Mismatched_values <- mapply(
  function(x, y) mismatch_count(shared[[paste0(x, "_aa")]],
                                shared[[paste0(y, "_codex")]]),
  match_fields$AA_output, match_fields$Codex_output
)
summary_table <- data.frame(
  Dataset = c("AA: final_list.csv", "Codex: final_data_codex.csv"),
  Rows = c(nrow(aa), nrow(codex)), Columns = c(ncol(aa), ncol(codex)),
  Countries = c(length(unique(aa$iso)), length(unique(codex$iso))),
  `Year range` = c(paste(range(aa$year), collapse = "–"),
                   paste(range(codex$year), collapse = "–")),
  `Duplicate country-year keys` = c(sum(duplicated(aa[key])),
                                    sum(duplicated(codex[key])))
)
```

## Comparison of the Final Data Sets

Table @tbl:overview shows that both files have one observation per observed
country-year, but they do not contain the same panel. The Codex output covers
186 countries from 2000 to 2019. The AA output covers 193 countries and also
includes 1999 observations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-overview
#| tbl-cap: "Structure of the two final data sets."
summary_table
```

Every one of the 3,720 Codex country-years occurs in the AA data. AA has 326
additional country-years: 186 from 1999 and 140 from 2000–2019 for `ASM`,
`GLP`, `MTQ`, `PLW`, `SCG`, `TUV`, and `TWN`. These seven countries are absent
from the covariates file. This difference reflects the merge strategy: AA uses
full joins and retains keys from every source, whereas Codex defines the
covariates file as the analytical panel and left-joins the remaining sources.

### Agreement in shared variables

The shared panel agrees exactly on all eight covariates, the four mortality
outcomes, and the lagged armed-conflict indicator. The mortality labels differ
only in presentation: AA's `matmor`, `infmor`, `neomor`, and `un5mor` equal
Codex's `maternal_mortality`, `infant_mortality`, `neonatal_mortality`, and
`under5_mortality`. AA's `armed_conflict_lag1` is identical to Codex's
`armed_conflict`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-matches
#| tbl-cap: "Value-level comparison on shared country-years."
match_fields
```

AA also retains `armed_conflict`, its current-year indicator. This can be
useful descriptively, but it is distinct from the lagged exposure in the Codex
final file.

### Disaster indicators

The main difference lies in disaster coding. AA has 1,206 missing values in
each of `earthquake` and `drought`. Within the shared panel, 1,020 missing AA
values for each indicator are zero in Codex; none are events in Codex. The
other 186 missing values occur in AA's extra 1999 observations.

Thus both workflows identify the same positive disaster events. AA treats a
country-year absent from the filtered disaster file as missing, while Codex
treats it as no recorded event. For an event-based data source, zero coding is
preferable: it preserves the covariate panel and prevents otherwise usable
country-years from being discarded by complete-case analysis.

## Comparison of Data Construction Methods

Both scripts reshape mortality data, derive disaster and conflict indicators,
and merge them with covariates. Their implementations differ in ways that
affect portability and interpretation. AA reads directly from `data/raw`, uses
interactive `View()`/`view()` calls, accepts only mortality columns beginning
with `X`, and uses abbreviated outcome names. Codex centralizes input reading,
supports `data/original` with a `data/raw` fallback, recognizes four-digit year
columns with or without `X`, and uses descriptive outcome names.

The conflict definitions also differ. AA totals deaths within `conflict_id` and
sets the indicator to one when any individual conflict reaches 25 deaths. Codex
totals deaths across conflicts within a country-year before applying the
25-death threshold. The supplied outputs have the same lagged values, but the
methods could diverge when several lower-fatality conflicts occur in one
country-year. AA matches a definition based on an individual `conflict_id`;
Codex matches a definition based on total annual country-level deaths.

Codex also checks duplicate country-year keys and reports dimensions, ranges,
frequencies, and missingness. It sorts final rows and avoids interactive-only
operations. AA has no equivalent automated validation, making it harder to
verify a rerun or identify unexpected changes in inputs.

## Reproducibility Assessment

Overall, **`codex_script.R` is the more reproducible workflow**. It explicitly
defines the analytical universe, returns the intended 2000–2019 panel, applies
a consistent no-event rule for disasters, validates country-year keys, and
provides diagnostics that document the output. It can also run
non-interactively from the repository root.

AA is still useful as an exploratory workflow and retains a current-year
conflict variable. Its separate `conflict_id` threshold may be substantively
preferable if that is the required definition. To be equally reproducible, it
would need an explicit final-panel rule, the disaster missing-to-zero rule,
non-interactive execution, and automated validation checks.

## Conclusion

The two workflows produce identical values for all shared covariates, mortality
outcomes, and lagged armed-conflict values. Their differences concern panel
construction and the treatment of absent disaster records. The Codex workflow
is recommended for the final analysis because it builds a complete,
covariate-based panel through transparent and auditable steps. Before analysis
is finalized, the project should explicitly state whether the 25-death rule
applies to each `conflict_id` or to total annual deaths in a country.
